title: Sleep as trust
hook: I will lay me down in peace and sleep (Psalm 4:8)
tomorrow: what does a day look like with all of this in it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Compline: the apple of his eye, kept close, then quiet. Now the last act of any day: lying down.
screen: `THE APPLE OF HIS EYE.` → `NOW, LYING DOWN.`

segments.voice: Two in the morning, eyes on the ceiling, the brain running tomorrow's list. Sleep won't take orders. Mark has a scene that's the opposite. A boat in a storm, waves breaking in until it's filling with water, the disciples terrified. And in the back of the boat, Jesus is asleep on a pillow. They shake him awake: “Master, carest thou not that we perish?”
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `A BOAT FILLING WITH WATER.` → `ASLEEP ON A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: So how can anyone sleep with so much unfinished? The Psalms answer with trust. Psalm four: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.” Psalm one hundred twenty-one gives the reason: “he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.” Someone else has the night watch. Lying down becomes a small act of trust. That's the sleep in the boat; when Jesus wakes, he says to the sea, “Peace, be still.” The Psalms are honest the other way too: “Thou holdest mine eyes waking.” This isn't a promise of a good night. It's a way to lie down. Now a neighbor. Muslims have bedtime words too. The hadith collection of al-Bukhari reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, would say on lying down, in effect: in your name, O God, I die and I live; and on waking, praise to God who gave us life after causing us to die. Both traditions treat sleep as a handing over, and waking as a gift. The honest difference: Muslims say those words following the Prophet's own practice, in their faith; Christian night prayer borrows Jesus' words from the cross in Luke: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.” Different words, different faiths, and in both, the night handed to God.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE HAS THE NIGHT WATCH.` · `PEACE, BE STILL.` · `IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.` · `INTO THY HANDS.` · then, large: `IN PEACE, SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit back and let your hands fall open in your lap, palms up. On each out-breath, set down one thing you were planning to keep watch over tonight. If you pray, borrow Psalm four as you go: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep.
Sleep as trust. Lying down as a way of handing the night to God, because someone else keeps watch.
Pocket this one: in peace, sleep, because the night watch isn't yours to keep. Rest well.

howItsDone: Some Christians say a line from Psalm 4 or Psalm 3 as they lie down, and some end the day by handing over their worries in prayer before sleep.

fork.setup: a parent's six-year-old asks why Grandma prays before bed. what's one sentence the parent could say at dinner?
options: she's asking God to promise nothing bad will ever happen.
she's making up for what she did wrong during the day.
she hands the night to God, so she can rest while God keeps watch.
fork.reveal: Psalm 4 and Psalm 121: lie down in peace, because the keeper neither slumbers nor sleeps. Muslims, too, hand over the night in the Prophet's bedtime words.

chat.says: last night at Pop's. can't sleep. what if he falls when i'm gone? and next year i'm gone gone.
options: You're not his only watch. Hand him over tonight, in peace, and plan the visits tomorrow.
Stay up and think it all through, so nothing gets missed while you're away.
Don't think about it. Worrying about family means you're not trusting God.
chat.meaning: Psalm 121 says the keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. Lying down hands the night over; tomorrow's plans can wait for morning.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: wisdom; Grace: Grace's last night at Pop's; she can't sleep, worried he'll fall when she's gone, and about leaving home next year).

Wisdom shape and the unity thread: the question (how can anyone sleep?), the Christian answer (the Psalms' trust; Jesus asleep in the boat), and a neighbor in its own words and source: the Prophet Muhammad's bedtime and waking words from Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrased ('in your name, O God, I die and I live'; 'praise to God who gave us life after causing us to die'). Shared: sleep as a handing over, waking as a gift. Honest difference: Muslims say those words following the Prophet's practice; Christian night prayer borrows Luke 23:46. No ranking, and the lesson says 'different faiths'. Confirm the hadith number (6312, also 6324 in some numberings), the paraphrase, and that a Muslim reader would find it fair.
'Christian night prayer borrows Jesus' words from the cross' refers to the Compline responsory 'Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit'; confirm the wording is fair across churches.
The line 'This isn't a promise of a good night' is there so the lesson doesn't shame people who can't sleep (Psalm 77:4).
